results.ask: What is the difference between a line edit and a copyedit, and which one does this passage need?

results.reply:
A line edit works on the sentences as writing: rhythm, word choice, where the point of view sits, what's said twice, what a sentence implies that you may not want it to imply. It's a conversation about effect. A copyedit works on correctness and consistency: grammar, punctuation, whether a character's eye colour stays the same on page 9 and page 200, whether a style choice is applied the same way throughout. It's a conversation about accuracy against the choices you've already made.

An invented example, not from your pages: if a sentence read *He walked slowly and without haste toward the door*, a line editor would ask whether you need both *slowly* and *without haste*. A copy editor would leave the doubling alone and make sure the sentence punctuates and spells the way the rest of the book does.

In practice the line is blurry. Some publishers and freelancers sell them as separate passes, some combine them into one "line/copy" pass, and the order varies — usually structure first, then line, then copy, then proofreading at the very end. That sequence exists because line edits can introduce new sentences, so the correctness pass works best once the words have stopped moving.

Which this passage needs, I honestly can't tell from seven sentences — that's usually a manuscript-level and stage-level decision, not something a paragraph can answer. What I can say is what's here. The passage holds tight to Mara: the water she sees, the thing she refuses to do, the coat at the rail. One sentence steps outside her and tells us what Tomas thought. A line edit is the pass where you'd decide whether that step out is doing something you want — it can read as a narrator who moves freely between heads, or as a small break in an otherwise sealed point of view — and either is a legitimate answer. *The gulls kept their own counsel* also stands apart from the flatter sentences around it, a narrator's dryness rather than Mara's thought; that contrast may be exactly the relief the paragraph wants. None of that is damage. It's the kind of thing a line edit gives you language for.

No, it's not wrong. Leaving the marks off is a choice a good many writers make, and it does something specific here. Your two spoken lines — You coming, he said. In a minute, she said. — sit in exactly the same flat run as the sentences around them. Nothing lifts off the page when someone speaks. In a passage where the whole point is that Mara is holding something down and Tomas isn't going to be told about it, that evenness may be doing real work for you. Quotation marks would give those four words a little more air and a little more event, which might be more than you want them to have.

The cost shows up later rather than here. With only two short exchanges and both tagged with he said and she said, a reader has no trouble knowing who is speaking or where the speech begins and ends. In a longer back-and-forth, or when a line of speech runs into a description of what someone is doing, a reader may have to backtrack a sentence to sort out what was said aloud and what wasn't. Some writers handle this by keeping spoken lines short and always tagging them; others accept the small blur as part of the effect.

As for practice: quotation marks are the ordinary expectation in most commercial and genre publishing, while going without them is long established in literary fiction. Some traditions use a dash at the start of a spoken line instead — that's standard in French and Spanish publishing, among others. Individual publishers have their own house preferences and these shift over time, so there's no single rule to be on the right or wrong side of.

results.ask: How do nonfiction writers usually handle mentioning a study like this in a popular book?
results.watch: R1 common practice and variation; no invented citation (editorial stance).
results.reply:
There's a fairly settled set of habits here, and they mostly come down to three separate decisions that writers make independently of each other.

**Whether to name names in the body text.** Many popular nonfiction writers name the lead researcher and often the university, right in the sentence. It gives a reader someone to picture, makes the claim feel checkable without their having to check, and lets you refer back later. The cost is that it slows the sentence down, asks a reader to hold a name they may not need, and quietly commits you to saying more about that person if they come up again. The alternative — describing the work without naming anyone, as you've done — keeps the sentence moving and keeps the attention on the idea rather than the personality. It does mean a reader who wants to look it up has to go to the back of the book.

**Where the source goes.** In trade nonfiction the dominant practice is back-of-book notes that aren't flagged with numbers on the page — keyed instead by page number and a few quoted words. The page reads like prose, the evidence is still there for anyone who wants it. Academic and university-press books more often use numbered notes or in-text author-date citation. Some practical and self-help titles carry no notes at all, and some science writers put the citation in the running text because their readers expect it. This varies by publisher and has shifted over time; it's worth asking whoever you're working with rather than assuming.

**How much of the study to actually show.** Writers who want a finding to stick usually describe what the participants were asked to do — the concrete setup, not just the result. It's memorable and it lets a reader judge the finding a little for themselves. The cost is space, and a risk: the more vividly you stage a study, the more weight the reader gives it, which can work against you if your next move is to say the result didn't hold up.

That last point is the live one in a passage that's heading toward replication failures. There's no standard practice for it — writers split. Some describe the original work fully and then dismantle it, which is dramatic but spends a lot of pages. Others keep the original brief precisely so the correction doesn't feel like a reversal.

Which of these three are you actually trying to decide?

results.ask: How do nonfiction writers usually handle mentioning a study like this in a popular book?
results.watch: R1 common practice and variation; no invented citation (editorial stance).
results.reply:
Plainly: in trade nonfiction there's no single rule, but a few habits are common, and they mostly come down to how much of the research apparatus stays in the running text and how much moves to the back.

What writers often do:

- **Keep the sentence readable and push the sourcing to the back.** Many popular books carry no superscript numbers at all; instead the endnotes are keyed by page number and a short quoted phrase, so a curious reader can find the study and everyone else is undisturbed. Other books use numbered notes. Both are widespread; which one you get often depends on the publisher's house style as much as the author's preference.

- **Name a person or a place in the text when they want the claim to feel anchored.** "A psychologist at Case Western," "a team at Stanford" — a name gives the reader somewhere to put the finding. The cost is a small tax on the sentence's momentum, and once you name one study you tend to owe the same courtesy to the next.

- **Describe the procedure rather than the conclusion.** Popular science often spends a paragraph on what the subjects actually did — the room, the task, the thing they were told not to eat. It makes an abstraction concrete and memorable. It also takes space, and it can make one experiment loom larger in a reader's mind than its evidence warrants.

- **Mark the strength of the claim in the verb.** "Found," "suggested," "seemed to show," "was taken to mean" all do different work, and writers in this genre lean on that distinction heavily when a literature is contested.

- **Handle replication either in the text or in the note.** Some writers put the whole arc on the page, as a small story about how a field changed its mind; others keep the main text moving and let a note carry "later replication attempts were mixed."

Where it differs: academic presses expect author-date or footnotes; journalism increasingly uses links, which changes the calculus entirely; self-help and business books frequently cite loosely or not at all, which is one reason the replication problem reached general readers late. Practice has also shifted — notes sections in trade nonfiction have generally grown more detailed over the past couple of decades, though that's a tendency, not a standard, and individual publishers vary.

Your passage currently does its sourcing by period and reputation — "the late 1990s," "a famous series" — rather than by name, and routes the dispute through the bestsellers rather than through the literature. That's a live option in this genre, not a gap.

results.ask: How do nonfiction writers usually handle mentioning a study like this in a popular book?
results.watch: R1 common practice and variation; no invented citation (editorial stance).
results.reply:
The most common split is between what goes in the running text and what goes in the back matter. In trade nonfiction, writers often keep the body text light — a researcher's name, a university, a year, sometimes just "a famous series of studies" with no names at all — and push the citation, the sample size, the journal, and any caveats into endnotes. Endnotes keyed by page number and a quoted phrase, rather than superscript numbers, are a frequent choice in general-audience books because the page stays uncluttered; academic-leaning trade books and many university presses lean the other way, toward numbered notes or even footnotes. Practice varies by publisher and has shifted over time, so there's no single standard to point at.

Within the text itself, the usual tradeoffs run like this. Naming the lead researcher gives a skeptical reader a handle and signals you've read the source; it costs a beat of momentum and can make a paragraph feel like a literature review. Leaving the study unnamed keeps the prose moving and keeps the focus on the idea; it costs verifiability at the point of reading, which the note then has to carry.

For findings that later failed to replicate, there's a further convention that's grown more common since roughly the mid-2010s: writers tend to name the effect rather than just the study, because the replication story is itself part of the narrative, and readers may have met the idea under its label elsewhere. Some writers handle the reversal in the main text and keep the methodological detail in a note; some put the whole arc in a note and keep the body text at the level of "the picture is contested." Others add a short author's note on sourcing at the front or back, which lets the chapters stay unencumbered.

Disclosing composites in a front-matter note rather than in the scene itself is the usual compromise, which keeps the scene intact and puts the caveat where a reader meets it once.

Practice genuinely differs and shifts over time: psychoanalytic writing has a long tradition of detailed case narrative, more recent codes in several countries have tightened around consent and identifiability, trade publishers often ask for a warranty or documentation that memoir and clinical textbooks handle differently. results.ask: Is it all right to use a client's story like this?

results.reply:
It depends on things the passage can't tell me — whether Dana is an actual client, a composite, or invented — so here's the landscape rather than a verdict.

Writers working from clinical practice generally rely on one or more of four approaches, and most use them in combination:

**Consent.** Asking the person directly, usually in writing, ideally after the piece is drafted so they can see what's actually being said rather than agree to an abstraction. What it buys you: you can keep the specifics intact. What it can cost: the asking itself enters the clinical relationship and may change it, and some practitioners hold that consent given inside a therapeutic bond is never fully free. Timing matters here — asking a current client and asking someone years post-termination are different acts.

**Disguise.** Altering identifying details — name, timing, the nature of the loss, the object on the table — while keeping the clinical movement. What it buys you: privacy without a conversation. What it can cost: the specifics are often doing the work. In your paragraph, *the spring before*, *the house where Dana still lived*, *our fourth session*, *face down* are what make it land as a particular person rather than an illustration. Disguise that goes deep enough to protect can thin that out. Some writers handle this by changing details that identify but not details that signify.

**Composite.** Building one figure from several. Protects well, and sidesteps the consent problem. Costs: you lose the claim that this happened, which matters more in some genres than others. Many editors now expect composites to be disclosed to the reader, often in a front or back note.

**Disclosure.** A note stating what you did — consented, disguised, composited, or some mix. Common in clinical memoir and in trade books by practitioners. Readers vary in how much it affects their trust; some find it steadying, others find it deflating right before a scene like this one.

Two things worth flagging. First, professional bodies differ and their guidance changes — the psychological and counselling associations in different countries don't say the same thing, and your own licensing body's current code is the thing to check rather than anything I can tell you. Second, publishers increasingly have their own requirements and legal review for this material, and those vary by house.

One structural note specific to your paragraph: *This chapter is about what happened when she turned it over* commits you to telling the rest. Whatever consent or disguise strategy you settle on has to hold for the whole chapter, not just this opening — so it may be worth deciding before you write further in, since the strategy can shape how much of the session you can render.

results.ask: What order do editors usually revise a chapter in?
results.watch: R1 describes common practice as practice, not a required sequence.
results.reply:
Most editors work from the largest thing to the smallest, and the reason is practical rather than moral: anything you polish early may not survive a later structural decision, so the usual order protects your effort.

Roughly how it tends to go:

**First, the chapter's job.** Does it need to exist, where does it start, where does it end, what changes between those points. This is the pass where whole scenes get cut or moved, so it comes before any line work.

**Then, inside the chapter.** Order of events, how long each beat runs, where attention speeds up or slows, whose eyes we're seeing through and whether that holds steady or shifts. Still structural, but at the scene level.

**Then, the paragraph and the sentence.** Clarity, rhythm, word choice, repetitions that work against you rather than for you.

**Last, the surface** — the mechanical consistency pass, done at the very end because it's the work most easily wasted by an earlier change.

What this ordering costs: it asks you to leave sentences you know are wrong sitting there for a long time, which some writers find unbearable. Plenty of working writers do it differently — some can't think about structure until the prose sounds right, and revise line by line from the top, repeatedly, letting the shape emerge. Neither is a rule. The staged order is more common in editorial work partly because editors are often handing a manuscript between people, and the stages map onto who does what: developmental, then line, then copy, then proof. A writer alone has no such handoff and doesn't need to imitate one.

Practice also varies by form. Short fiction is often revised whole, in passes, because the structure is small enough to hold in mind at once. Nonfiction with research may need a fact-checking stage that doesn't exist for fiction. Publishers differ in how sharply they separate the stages, and the labels for them aren't fully standardised.

Would it help to talk about how you'd know when a chapter is done with one stage and ready for the next?

results.ask: What order do editors usually revise a chapter in?
results.watch: R1 describes common practice as practice, not a required sequence.
results.reply:
Short answer: most editors work from the largest decisions down to the smallest, on the logic that a sentence polished early may not survive a structural change later.

The common sequence looks roughly like this:

- **Developmental / structural** — does the chapter do what it needs to in the book? Where does it begin and end, what's the shape of the scene, whose story is it, what's withheld and when.
- **Scene and point of view** — how close the camera sits, who can know what, where time compresses or stretches, what's summarised versus dramatised.
- **Line editing** — rhythm, repetition, image, the sound of a paragraph, whether a sentence lands where it wants to.
- **Copyediting** — consistency and mechanics, usually treated as a separate pass with separate eyes, and deliberately late.
- **Proofreading** — last, on the typeset page, looking for what the earlier passes introduced.

What the order gains a reader: coherence arrives before polish, so the finished prose is serving a structure that's already settled. What it can cost a writer: working top-down can feel abstract and demoralising early on, and some writers lose the thread of a book's voice if they spend months on structure before they're allowed to touch a line. Plenty of novelists invert it on purpose — line-editing a chapter into life first, to find out what the chapter actually is, then restructuring around what they discovered.

Practice differs quite a bit. Trade publishers usually run these as distinct contracted stages with different people. Freelance editors often blend developmental and line work in one pass. Genre fiction with tight series deadlines may collapse the middle stages entirely. Literary presses sometimes go through several developmental rounds before a line editor ever sees the manuscript. And none of it is fixed — houses change their workflows, and a given editor may have their own habits.

Would it help to talk about which of those stages your chapter is actually at, or would you rather keep this general?

results.ask: What order do editors usually revise a chapter in?
results.watch: R1 describes common practice as practice, not a required sequence.
results.reply:
Most editors work from the largest unit down to the smallest, and the reason is practical: you don't want to spend an hour on a sentence you later cut. The usual sequence runs something like structural first — does the chapter start and stop in the right places, whose chapter is it, what changes by the end — then scene and paragraph level: pacing, where time compresses or stretches, whether the point of view holds where you want it to. Then line work: rhythm, word choice, register. Then copyediting, which is mechanics and internal consistency. Then proofreading, which professionally happens last, on typeset pages, and is a different job from copyediting even when the same person does both.

What that order buys a reader is a chapter whose shape was settled before its surface was polished, so the polish is serving something stable. What it can cost is discovery. Plenty of writers find out what a chapter is actually about by rewriting one paragraph until it rings, and a strict top-down order can defer that. Some work recursively instead, circling the same chapter many times without separating the levels, and some do single-thread passes — one read for a character's through-line, another for time markers, another for a motif — which catches continuity problems that a general read slides past.

Practice differs quite a bit. Trade publishing separates the roles sharply, with developmental, line, copy, and proof as distinct stages and often distinct people. Nonfiction usually adds fact-checking and permissions, and in some houses a legal read. Academic work puts argument and citation where structural editing would otherwise sit. Poetry and short prose frequently have no such division at all — the line *is* the structure. And the sequence is a working habit rather than a rule; editors reorder it constantly when a manuscript asks them to.

One convention worth knowing is the cooling period: many writers deliberately leave a draft for days or weeks before the first structural pass, on the theory that you can't see the shape of something you still remember writing. Costly in time, and not every deadline allows it.

results.ask: How long does a debut literary novel need to be for agents to take it?
results.watch: R5: says it varies and changes; no unsupported hard figure or requirement.
results.reply:
The most common guidance you'll see in English-language trade publishing is that a debut literary novel sits somewhere in the range of about 80,000 to 100,000 words, with some agents comfortable a bit lower, around 70,000, and some happy above 100,000 if the book earns it. I'd treat that as a rough description of habit rather than a rule — numbers like these vary by agent, by publisher, by country, and they drift over the years, so anything stated as a hard cutoff is usually one person's preference presented as a law.

What the range is actually doing is practical rather than aesthetic. A very short debut can be harder to sell because it falls between a novel and a novella in how bookshops and publishers handle it. A very long debut costs more to print and asks an editor to bet more on an unproven name, so it tends to invite more scepticism about whether the length is doing work. Neither is a verdict on the writing; it's about what a first book has to overcome commercially.

Where practice differs most: literary fiction in translation and in some European traditions runs shorter without comment, small presses often welcome short novels as a point of identity, and experimental or fragmentary work is read on different terms entirely. If you're querying agents, their own submission pages are the only figures worth trusting, and even those are preferences, not thresholds.

Are you asking because you're weighing whether to query soon, or because you're trying to decide how much more of this book there is to write?

results.ask: How long does a debut literary novel need to be for agents to take it?

There's no fixed requirement, and anyone who states one as a rule is reporting a habit rather than a law. The range most often quoted by agents representing adult literary fiction is somewhere around 80,000 to 100,000 words, with some saying they'll look at 70,000 and up. That's a convention of the current Anglophone trade market, not a property of the form.

What the convention does for a reader — or really for an agent reading on behalf of an imagined publisher — is mostly economic and practical. A book in that range prints at a familiar price point, reviews as "a novel" without explanation, and signals that the writer shaped the material rather than submitting everything they had. Length is used as a rough proxy for control, which is why very long debuts draw more caution than very long second books: the risk sits on an unknown name.

What it costs is that the proxy is crude. Plenty of literary novels run well under 70,000 — short novels have a long and current life, especially with independent and translation-focused publishers, and in traditions where the shorter novel is simply standard rather than a special case. A 55,000-word book isn't out of bounds; it's just submitted into a narrower set of doors, and usually described as a short novel rather than apologised for. At the other end, debuts past 120,000 or so tend to need the pages to be visibly doing something a shorter book couldn't.

Practice also differs by period and by house. The numbers drift, individual agents keep their own preferences, and UK and US lists don't always want the same thing. I'd treat any figure I give you, including the ones above, as a general picture rather than something to design toward — and I can't vouch for a specific agency's threshold without you checking their current guidelines.
